newsitem.title: INDIA: India call dips on inflows from forex intervention.
newsitem.headline: India call dips on inflows from forex intervention.

text.p: Indian call money ended Tuesday at 9.75-9.25 percent, off the day's opening 9.5-10.25 percent on expectations of improved liquidity, dealers said.
They said spot dollar purchases by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) on Monday and Tuesday would inject rupees into the banking system over the next two days and bring call money rates down.
Dealers said RBI dollar purchases could have been in the region of $300-400 million over the two days.

"This will boost liquidity and cool rates down," said a dealer at a foreign bank. "But the actual problem over the last couple of days has been that lenders seem to be holding back and pushing up rates."
Call money rates have been above 9.0 percent since last Friday after trading below 1.0 percent for most of April.
Dealers said most of Tuesday's trade was between 9.5 and 10.25 percent before rates eased in the afternoon.
One-month money was quoted at 8.5-10.0 percent and three months at 9.0-11.0 percent, they said.
Perceptions of easing liquidity triggered buying interest in government securities and prices rose, dealers said.
But they said volumes were thin with Tuesday's trades worth 2.16 billion rupees against Monday's 2.77 billion.

Among actively traded securities, the 13.50 percent 1997 government stock rose to 101.50 rupees from its last traded 101.42, the 13.65 percent 1998 to 103.28 from 103.20 and the 13.80 percent 2002 to 105.20 from 105.05, dealers said.
Dealers also reported trades in the 13.80 percent 2002 at 103.87 rupees, in the 13.12 percent 1999 at 102.10 and in the 11.64 percent 2000 at 98.30.
